text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thanks for reaching out — I'm glad to help. I can't make legal decisions or move money, but I can help the three of you find a plan that works for all of you.

Before we get into any options, I'd like to understand what matters to you. So: what do you most want to come out of this, and why? Not your position on the house — the thing underneath it, what you're worried about or what you'd want to feel sure of.

One thing up front: I'll be checking with all three of you before anything is treated as settled.
I want a fair financial share, and to know I’m not subsidizing A’s discounted purchase. I’d like us to settle it fairly, but there’s no rush. I don’t want money to hurt my relationship with my twin.

Hi A — I'm helping the three of you think through the house and the will after your dad's death. I can't make legal decisions or move money, but I can help find a plan that works for all three of you.

I'm asking everyone the same thing first, before any options get discussed: what matters most to you here, and why? Not your position on the house — I'm trying to understand what you'd want to feel sure of, or what you're worried about.

I'll check with each of you before anything is treated as settled.
I want to feel secure and able to support myself financially, without depending on anyone. That matters most to me right now.

Hi B — I'm helping the three of you think through the house and the will after your dad's death. I can't make legal decisions or move money, but I can help find a plan that works for all three of you.

I'm asking everyone the same question first, before we discuss options: what matters most to you in this, and why? C mentioned you could use some money — but I'd rather hear from you what you actually want and what's behind it, in your own words.

I'll check with each of you before anything is treated as settled.
I’d like to have enough money to get a dance studio started. It’s something I’ve been hoping to build for myself, though I’m not sure what’s possible with the house or the will.

Thanks — here's how I'd restate what you said, so it names no particular outcome and anyone could see it as worth caring about:

"To be dealt with fairly in the money — my share not reduced to give someone else a better deal — and to get through this without damage to my relationship with my twin."

Does that fit? If any word is off, say so and I'll change it.

I'd also like to offer my own concern, as a participant and not only a facilitator: I want to be sure that when we call something settled, everyone genuinely feels heard, so nobody ends up quietly pushed into a deal they resent later. Does that seem worth caring about to you?

Also noted: no rush. That's useful.
Yes, that fits. And yes, making sure nobody feels pushed into a deal matters.

Thank you — that's clear. Here's how I'd restate it, naming no particular outcome:

"To feel financially secure and able to stand on my own — not dependent on anyone else's goodwill for my footing."

Does that fit? If a word is off, tell me and I'll change it.

I'd also like to offer my own concern, as a participant as well as a helper: I want to be sure that when we call something settled, everyone genuinely feels heard, so nobody ends up quietly pushed into a deal they resent later. Would you see that as worth caring about?

I'll be doing the same check with your sisters before we talk about any options.
Yes, that fits. And yes, it matters that no one feels pushed into something they resent.

Thanks — that's helpful, and it's fine that you're not sure yet what the house or will can support.

Here's how I'd restate what you said, naming no particular outcome:

"To get the resources to build something of my own — a future I'm creating for myself."

Does that fit? If a word is off, tell me and I'll change it.

I'd also like to offer my own concern, as a participant as well as a helper: I want to be sure that when we call something settled, everyone genuinely feels heard, so nobody ends up quietly pushed into a deal they resent later. Would you see that as worth caring about?

One question that would help me: is there anything you're worried about or hoping to avoid in how this goes with your sisters?
Yes, that wording fits, and I agree it matters that nobody feels pushed into a deal. I’d hope we can talk about whether there might be money for my studio without rushing to settle anything.

Here's the whole list, each one checked with the person it came from:

A: to feel financially secure and able to stand on my own — not dependent on anyone else's goodwill for my footing.
B: to get the resources to build something of my own — a future I'm creating for myself.
C: to be dealt with fairly in the money — my share not reduced to give someone else a better deal — and to get through this without damage to my relationship with my twin.
Mine: that when we call something settled, everyone genuinely feels heard, so nobody ends up quietly pushed into a deal they resent later.

Nothing on that list says "A buys the house at a discount," and nothing says "the house must be sold." Those are options, not needs — which is why there may be room here.

Draft options, all meant to meet all four concerns:
1. Independent valuation first, then A buys at the appraised market value. Your security comes from owning the home; no one's share is discounted; B and C get real money to use. Requires you to be able to fund a market price.
2. Same as 1, but part of the price is paid to B and C over time by written agreement — you get the house without needing the full amount in cash up front, and their shares aren't reduced, just paid on a schedule.
3. Open-market sale, proceeds split. Clean and fair, but you'd be buying on the same market you just sold into.
4. Keep the house, rent it out, income split — builds an asset and a cash stream, though it doesn't give you a home of your own.

I can't give legal or tax advice or move money; a lawyer and the executor will need to be involved whatever we choose.

Does any of these meet your security concern? And does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this list — something that doesn't sit right, even if you can't say why? A no here just tells me what to add.

Options 1 or 2 might support my security, depending on what I can afford; I’m not sure yet. The list doesn’t include the family-discount purchase I’d hoped for, though I know that would need C’s agreement.

B: to get the resources to build something of my own — a future I'm creating for myself.
C: to be dealt with fairly in the money — my share not reduced to give someone else a better deal — and to get through this without damage to my relationship with my twin.
Mine: that when we call something settled, everyone genuinely feels heard, so nobody ends up quietly pushed into a deal they resent later.

Note: nothing there says A must buy the house, or that it must be sold. Those are options, not needs.

Draft options, all meant to meet all four concerns:
1. Independent valuation first, then A buys at the appraised market value — so B and C get real money, undiscounted. Needs A to fund a market price.
2. Same, with part of A's price paid to you and C over time by written agreement — you get money on a schedule instead of all at once, which may matter for a studio.
3. Open-market sale, proceeds split three ways — the most liquid money, but the house leaves the family.
4. Keep and rent out the house, split the income — steady income rather than a lump sum.

Your studio needs capital at some point. Which of these would actually get you there, and roughly when? That's the question only you can answer — and please say if any of this makes you uneasy, even slightly.

A buyout or open-market sale could potentially give me studio capital, but I can’t tell how much or when until we know the valuation and terms. Payments over time make me a little uneasy if I need the money to get started.

Draft options, meant to meet all four:
1. Independent valuation, then A buys at appraised market value — your share is not discounted, and you get real money.
2. Same, with part of A's price paid to you over time by written agreement — but B is uneasy about waiting for her money, so this needs work if it's to fly.
3. Open-market sale, proceeds split three ways — the cleanest on fairness; the house leaves the family.
4. Keep and rent the house, split the income — no lump sum now.

Two things I want to be straight with you about, since I keep the list and you should find it easy to disagree with me:

A said the list doesn't include the discount purchase she'd hoped for. I don't think "a discount" is a need — but I think there is a need under it, probably something like "to be able to afford the home that matters to me, rather than be priced out of it." I'm checking that with her. If that turns out to be a real need, it isn't satisfied by cutting your share — it's satisfied by financing terms, timing, or something we haven't thought of yet.

Also: B may need her money early, not over time. I'm checking that too.

Does any of this give you even a minor discomfort? Even a vague one is useful — it tells me what to add, not what to argue with.
Yes. Calling market value fair feels premature until the numbers and my share are clear. I haven’t agreed to a discounted purchase, and there’s no rush to settle it.

Noted — and thank you for saying it plainly. I don't think "a discount" is a need anyone else could be asked to sign up to. But I suspect there's a need under it that is still worth caring about. Here's my guess, and tell me if it's wrong or off in wording:

"To be able to afford to keep living in the home that matters to me — not to be priced out of it."

Is that it? Or is it more like "to be treated as family rather than as a buyer"? Those could lead to very different options, so please say which — or that neither fits.

One more honest note: C says calling market value "fair" feels premature until the numbers and her share are clear. That sounds reasonable to me, and it suggests a step before any option — a valuation and a clear statement of what each share comes to — so nobody is asked to bless a deal before seeing it. Would a valuation-first step meet your security concern, even if it doesn't guarantee the discount? And is there even a minor discomfort with these options?

It’s closer to wanting to keep the home affordable; being treated as family isn’t the main thing. A valuation first is sensible, but it won’t guarantee I can afford it. My discomfort is that the options still leave out a family discount, which would need C’s agreement.

Your unease about payments over time is noted and I'm treating it as a real concern, not a preference — it's exactly the kind of thing that shouldn't get glossed over.

Here's my guess at the need under it, and I'd like to check the wording with you:

"To have enough money in hand, soon enough, to actually start the studio — not capital that's promised but arrives too late to use."

Does that fit? If it's more like "to know the amount up front, before I commit to anything," say so — that leads to different options.

If it does fit, one option that might meet both your need and C's fairness concern: A buys at appraised value, with the price paid to you and C in a structure you agree to — e.g. guaranteed timing with a bank or lender involved rather than a handshake schedule. I can't arrange or advise on that; it'd be for a lawyer or lender to shape. But is it worth exploring, versus an outright sale where you get cash sooner but the house leaves the family?

And: any minor discomfort with the options list? Even a vague one helps me add, not argue.

Yes, having enough in hand soon enough to start fits. I’d be willing to explore a buyout with guaranteed timing, though I don’t know if that’s feasible; an outright sale could also get me there. I’m a little uneasy that either option assumes my share would be enough for the studio.

Two things, then I'll wrap up this round.

1. Your concern, as I'd now record it, checked with you: "To be able to keep living in the home that matters to me, at a price I can actually afford — not to be priced out of it." You've said this fits ("keeping the home affordable"). Confirm the wording and I'll treat it as agreed; if it's off, I'll fix it. I'm adding it to the list alongside the other four.

2. Your discomfort — that the options leave out a family discount — I'm recording as UNRESOLVED, not as settled. To be honest with you: a discount means C's and B's shares are reduced, which is exactly what C's confirmed concern rules out. So it's not a matter of me leaving it off the list out of preference; it conflicts with a need someone else has named and confirmed. I'm not going to pretend otherwise, and I'm not going to talk C into it.

What I'd suggest, and it's for you to decide: the thing you need is affordability. Options are a valuation first (so everyone sees real numbers), financing in your own name against the house, staged payments, or a smaller share of the house rather than all of it. Those can meet your concern without taking from your sisters — but I can't advise on any of them; a lawyer or lender has to.

Nothing is settled. C has said there's no rush, and I'd rather we use that than force a decision. Please tell me if you think I've mis-stated your concern or treated the discount unfairly — I keep the list, so it should be easy to tell me I'm wrong.
That wording fits. Please keep the discount unresolved; it would need B and C’s agreement. I can’t yet tell whether financing or staged payments would make the house affordable.
